claims.text: The initial Ti–Ni-based high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution without a controlled secondary-phase dispersion.
Adding 0.5–1 at% carbon during vacuum arc melting will promote in-situ formation of nanoscale carbide particles.
Homogenization at approximately 1050°C followed by controlled cooling or aging will optimize particle nucleation and growth.
The intervention will produce an evenly dispersed nanoscale secondary-particle population in the single-phase matrix.
TiC is a candidate particle phase produced by the intervention.
Ni3Ti is presented as a candidate nanoscale carbide particle produced by the intervention.
The resulting particles will remain stable during elevated-temperature deformation.
The nanoparticles will obstruct dislocation motion during high-temperature deformation.
The nanoparticles will obstruct grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature deformation.
Obstruction of dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding will improve elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance.
The carbon-doped, heat-treated alloy will have significantly higher yield strength from 600°C to 950°C than the control alloy.
The carbon-doped, heat-treated alloy will have improved creep resistance from 600°C to 950°C relative to the control alloy.
The predicted improvement depends on obtaining an optimized particle size distribution and volume fraction.
The proposed scope is Ti–Ni-based high-entropy alloys in which titanium and nickel are the primary constituents.
Excessive particle coarsening or formation of unwanted brittle phases would fall outside the desired processing window.
The applicable mechanical-testing temperature range is limited to 600–950°C.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as lacking both carbon and the subsequent optimized heat treatment, whereas the falsification experiment specifies a carbon-free control with otherwise identical processing. These define different controls and could confound the separate effects of carbon and heat treatment.

The particle population is repeatedly characterized as carbide particles, but Ni3Ti is included as an example alongside TiC without distinguishing carbide precipitation from intermetallic precipitation.
